Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:14: It further says on: the "havalim" of the Other Side, concerning which it is said, "they are vanity (hevel), a work of delusion" (Jeremiah 10:15) — these "havalim" ascend through vile speech of the mouth and falsehoods, and they all ascend toward the brain; there are sun, moon, stars, and constellations in firmaments that are kelipot, concerning which it is said, "Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity" (Isaiah 5:18), and concerning them it is said, "for the heavens shall vanish away like smoke..." (Isaiah 51:6), "then the moon shall be ashamed and the sun confounded" (Isaiah 24:23); and there are many "havalim" for them, all full of falsehood and vanity, and whoever utters false words, how many destroying angels open their wings to receive them — this is what is written, "for a bird of the heavens shall carry the voice" (Ecclesiastes 10:20), and these utterances are the building blocks of several structures — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:15: These passages make clear the difference between the holy "hevel" of Torah study and the like, and the unholy "hevel" — that the unholy "hevel" ascends to the kelipah and builds false structures, "vanity, a work of delusion," as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:16: The general rule is that according to how a person builds in this world, there his soul ascends after his death, as explained in the passage from Parashat Beshalach that we quoted — unless he returns in complete and strong repentance to nullify all those firmaments and lands he built on the side of the kelipah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:17: It further says, on (Tikkunim 118a), that all the "havalim" of prayers ascend and are bound in the holy "hevel," which is the Shechinah, and there is a "hevel" of idle talk that is in the kelipah, in these words, in brief: there is a "hevel" concerning which it is said, "his brother, Hevel" (Genesis 4:2); and there is a "hevel" in prayers and good acts of worship; and there is a "hevel" of idle talk, empty words, concerning which it is said, "vanity (hevel), a work of delusion..." — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:18: Further on (there) it explains that there is, between these two "havalim," a middle "hevel" that is neither holy nor impure, but mundane talk — the necessity of using worldly words — over which we say "who separates between holy and mundane"; and over the external "hevel" we say "between Israel and the other nations."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:19: Now, when a person considers what we have written above — that a person's obligation to sanctify his limbs is because in each and every limb of his the Name YHVH is found, and by sanctifying that limb he sanctifies the Name — all the more so must he be obligated to sanctify his mouth, in which the Name YHVH is found in several aspects: whether in the limbs producing speech, and the five points of articulation participate in the production of speech, and it must be that each and every one contains the Name YHVH, since they are distinct organs — throat, palate, tongue, teeth, lips; or in the aspect of voice and speech itself, in which the Name YHVH exists, as explained above. And so it is fitting for him to consider, since in prayer he utters several mentions [of the Name] from his mouth, whether in psalms or in blessings, and therefore it is fitting to sanctify his mouth so that the Name YHVH not go forth from a blemished mouth.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:20: And in the Tikkunim (132a) it says, in these words: a twisted mouth — the Holy One, blessed be He, does not rest within it, for it is a blemish, and all the more so if its speech is twisted; of it is said, "that which is crooked cannot be made straight" (Ecclesiastes 1:15). Mouth and heart correspond to the Written Torah and the Oral Torah; voice and speech emerging from them both are Vav-Heh, and they must be uttered with the awe and love of Yod-Heh; and if not, YHVH does not rest there — so far his words. What it says, "mouth and heart correspond to Torah," means that the heart is the Written Torah and the mouth corresponds to the Oral Torah — for just as the mouth reveals what is hidden in the heart, so the Oral Torah reveals what is concealed in the Written Torah. The intent of this is to teach us that one's mouth and heart should be equal, and by this he unifies; but if he speaks one thing with his mouth and another in his heart, he causes separation and cuts the plantings [an idiom for heresy/severance].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:21: From this passage it is understood that wherever there is a blemish in one's mouth or speech, the Name YHVH does not rest there, and one becomes liable to reincarnation (as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, have taught us, as mentioned above) to rectify what he has twisted. And just as the punishment is great, so the reward for one who sanctifies his mouth is great, for he sanctifies the Shechinah, called "mouth," and therefore merits the holy spirit, as we explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:22: Regarding mundane speech, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, warned us in the Mishnah, saying (Avot 1:17), "I have found nothing better for the body than silence." This is explained "for the body" to mean for matters of the body, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Chullin (89a), on the verse, "Do you indeed speak righteousness, you silent ones?" (Psalms 58:2, homiletically read), in these words: Rabbi Yitzchak said, what is [the meaning of] "Do you indeed speak righteousness, you silent ones? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of man?" — what is a person's occupation in this world? He should make himself as one silent. One might think even regarding matters of Torah — the verse teaches, "speak righteousness." One might think he should be proud [of his silence regarding Torah] — the verse teaches, "do you judge uprightly, O sons of man" — so far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:23: And so King Solomon, peace be upon him, warned us of this, saying, "Do not be rash with your mouth, and let not your heart be hasty to utter a word before God; for God is in heaven, and you upon earth; therefore let your words be few" (Ecclesiastes 5:1). One must be precise, for how does he give a reason for his words being few based on the fact that God is in heaven and you are on earth — for on the contrary, this would seem to indicate a withdrawal of providence, and it would have been fitting for him to say words indicating providence — that God is [both] in heaven and on earth, in the manner of "who humbles Himself to look upon the heavens and upon the earth" (Psalms 113:6). And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in the Sifrei (Ha'azinu 4): Solomon said, so long as even the weakest of the weak above defeats the mighty, when it is from below and above, the mightiest of the mighty all the more so; and so it says, "Do you thus requite the Lord?" (Deuteronomy 32:6) — so far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:24: What appears to us in explaining this verse — even if it be at length, because of the great benefit reaching the tongue from it, we shall not refrain — is this. One must be precise about the wording "al tevahel al picha" ("do not be rash concerning your mouth") — why does it not say simply "do not be rash [with] your mouth" or "[in] your mouth"? Why the extra word "al" ("upon/concerning")?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:25: Rather, the matter is this: the mouth encompasses the five points of articulation of the letters, as is explained in the Tikkunim (132a), in these words: five rectifications are in the mouth, of which it is stated in Sefer Yetzirah: Aleph-Het-Ayin-Heh, Bet-Vav-Mem-Peh, Gimel-Yod-Kaf-Kof, Dalet-Tet-Lamed-Nun-Tav, Zayin-Samech-Shin-Reish-Tzadi; and through them complete stones are built for the Holy One, blessed be He, in many prayers and acts of worship; and concerning them Jacob said, "and he lay down (vayishkav) in that place" (Genesis 28:11) — vayishkav [broken into] Vav-Yod-Shin, Kaf-Bet, in that place — Yod-Shin: "to cause those who love Me to inherit substance (yesh)" (Proverbs 8:21); Kaf-Bet: "with you (bach) Israel shall bless" (Genesis 48:20) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:26: And in Sefer Yetzirah (2:6) it says that the Holy One, blessed be He, fixed in our mouth twenty-two letters in five points of articulation: twenty-two foundational letters, engraved in the voice, hewn out in the wind, fixed in the mouth in five places — Aleph-Het-Ayin-Heh, Bet-Vav-Mem-Peh, Dalet-Tet-Lamed-Nun-Tav, Zayin-Samech-Tzadi-Reish-Shin, Gimel-Yod-Kaf-Kof. My teacher, peace be upon him, explains that the word "fixed (kevu'ot) in the mouth," stated there, indicates a great matter to us — that the reality of these five points of articulation is rooted very high above, in the head, and they are the root of all existing things, as explained in the Idra; but they descend and are revealed from world to world in the aspects of Atzilut, Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah, and the Holy One, blessed be He, out of His love for man, fixed these letters in his mouth so that he can cleave to his Creator — for when he mentions these letters below, in his Torah study or prayer, he shakes and arouses above the supernal roots. This is the meaning of the word "fixed" (kavua) — like one who fastens a chain, one end in one place and the other end in another place, so that even though that place is far off, when a person shakes the end of the chain in his hand, he shakes the whole chain, however great it may possibly be. And so it likewise says at the end of Sefer Yetzirah (6:8): He bound twenty-two letters with his tongue, and the Place revealed His secret to him. The word "bound" (kesher) likewise indicates what is expounded from the word "fixed" (kavua).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:27: By this we understand the greatness of the early ones, peace be upon them, whose prayer was heard immediately — because they were careful not to blemish the twenty-two letters, which are the five points of articulation fixed in their mouths, with idle talk and other things that blemish the tongue; therefore their prayer would burst through the firmaments and ascend higher and higher to arouse mercy. And so it is said in the Zohar (Parashat Shemot 14b), that at the time Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, peace be upon him, was occupied with Torah, several thousand and myriads of ministering angels would listen to his voice; the reason being that because the points of articulation emerging from their mouths were pure, they would bind and unify all the worlds, for the voice and speech emerging from their mouths would become a satisfaction above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:28: However, when there is a blemish in the five points of articulation, the breath of prayer and Torah emerging from his mouth emerges through a blemish and an adhesion [terefah, a defect making an animal unfit], and it cannot be unified above, since "whatever has a blemish shall not come near" (Leviticus 21:18). And so it says in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 227b), in these words: and just as those five wings of the lung are all open without adhesion, to receive this voice, so too the five rectifications of the mouth must all be open without adhesion, with the five rectifications, which are: Aleph-Het-Ayin-Heh in the throat, Bet-Vav-Mem-Peh in the lips, Gimel-Yod-Kaf-Kof in the palate, Dalet-Tet-Lamed-Nun-Tav in the tongue, Zayin-Samech-Shin-Reish-Tzadi in the teeth — and speech should be within them without any adhesion or hindrance at all — this is what is written, "and it was, before he had finished speaking, that, behold, Rebecca came out..." (Genesis 24:15) — this is prayer, which is speech, and concerning it is said, "if my prayer is fluent (shegurah) in my mouth, I know it is accepted; but if there is an adhesion, and it comes out in a mixture [confusion], I know it is torn (mutraf)" — for an adhesion (sircha) makes it "torn" (treifah) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:29: Now, with this introduction, we understand the verse: in saying "al tevahel al picha," the intent is that "your mouth" (picha) refers to the collective of the five points of articulation, as explained; and "tevahel" (be rash/confounded) means that no blemish should be found in them, which would be a confounding (behalah) and a kelipah — and the kelipah is the external part, which is [the extra word] "al" ("upon/concerning") "your mouth" — which is superfluous, coming upon the five points of articulation. My colleague Rabbi Moshe Bayurokas, peace be upon him, said a fine thing regarding this matter — that it is known (Parashat Naso 134a) that from the supernal mouth a "hevel" (breath) emerges, as we explained above, and the intent of "al tevahel" is that you should not turn the "hevel" (breath) into "behalah" (confusion), which is the kelipah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:30: Now, in the manner explained regarding "al picha," our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in Tanchuma, of blessed memory: this is what the verse says, "al tevahel al picha, and let not your heart be hasty to utter a word..." — this refers to people who curse the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He. Come and see: when the upper and lower beings were created, they were created with half the Name, as it is said, "for in Yah, the Lord, is the strength of worlds" (Isaiah 26:4) — why were they not created with the whole [Name]? Because the world is not worthy to mention the whole Name of the Holy One, blessed be He. Woe to the creatures who curse the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He! See what is written regarding offerings: "an offering to the Lord," "a burnt offering to the Lord" — it does not say "to the Lord, an offering, to the Lord, a burnt offering" — yet people curse and blaspheme My Name; therefore it is said, "al tevahel al picha." This clearly shows that they came to explain the word "al tevahel" [with] "al" [as an extra element] — for the "behalah" (confounding, cursing) is superfluous upon the mouth, which is not needed by a person, since your mouth is certainly created for the sake of the five points of articulation within it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:31: It might further be said — it is known that the speech that comes to a person is from the Shechinah, as it is said, "Who has made man's mouth? Or who makes the dumb...? Have not I, the Lord?" (Exodus 4:11), and the word "anochi" (I) can be explained as [referring to] the supernal Shechinah and the lower Shechinah, as is explained in the Tikkunim (74b), that concerning them it is said "Anochi, Anochi" [twice] — but mostly it refers to the supernal Shechinah, from where comes "I am (Anochi) the Lord your God," as is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 256b). The intent of this is: do not blemish the attribute that is "upon your mouth" — from where it came to be a mouth, for the five points of articulation are from the mystery of the supernal Heh, and from there too comes the power of speech, as it is said, "or who makes the dumb..." And if we explain it as referring to the Shechinah, "and she is upon your mouth," we would explain "have not I, the Lord" as [referring to] voice and speech, and the rest of the details of the verse fit properly with these attributes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:32: I heard from the mouth of my teacher, peace be upon him, that a person's mouth is above ten [handbreadths, i.e., not subject to the same limitations], and the voice and speech emerging from his mouth, if it is in holiness, immediately the Shechinah is bound to it — for the Shechinah does not descend below ten [handbreadths] (Sukkah 5a). In this matter, the wording of the verse "al picha" is now precise — that the Shechinah is "upon your mouth," for your mouth is above ten; this is [the meaning of] "if you lie among the sheepfolds" (bein hashefatayim) (Psalms 68:14), which is explained in the Tikkunim (45a) to mean that he should lay the Shechinah, who is "Em" (mother), between his lips (bein sfatav), in order to unify her.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:33: Further, we already quoted in the Gate of Love (ch. 9) what Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, peace be upon him, says in his commandments (Zohar Parashat Naso 122b), that the Shechinah is "the utterance of the mouth of the Lord" by which a person is sustained, in these words, in brief: and she is a "hevel" (breath) that enters a person's mouth without toil and without labor — Heh of [the word] "behibar'am" ("when they were created"). Through this passage "al picha" fits well.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:34: "And let not your heart be hasty to utter a word before God" — the matter is that speech emerges from the heart, as is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna several times (Parashat Naso 121b, Parashat Pinchas 227b), and in the Tikkunim (28a), in these words: the heart is a consuming fire, from the right ear of the heart, which is toward the liver, and from it emerges speech — this is what is written, "Is not My word like a fire, says the Lord" (Jeremiah 23:29); and were it not for the wings of the lung that blow upon the heart, it would burn the whole body — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:35: Therefore it says, "and let not your heart be hasty to utter a word," since speech emerges from it, and the speech emerging from it is [associated with] judgment, as Rashbi explains that the heart is fire, and speech is said of it, "Is not My word like a fire." And the speech goes forth "before God" (lifnei ha'Elohim), for God is [a term of] judgment, since this world's essential creation was in judgment, as it is said, "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1); and when He saw that it could not endure, He joined with it the attribute of mercy (see Bereshit Rabbah 12:15) — but this is only a partnership, in the general sense, for its essential creation was in judgment, and it stands upon judgment, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Tzav 30b), that every single day judgment is suspended over the world, because the world was created upon judgment and stands upon it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:36: It might also be said, regarding "before God" (lifnei ha'Elohim), that this teaches us regarding [divine] providence, that one should know that when he speaks, the King of kings of kings, God, hears our words — as the Rambam, peace be upon him, explains regarding awe (Guide of the Perplexed, part 3, ch. 52) — that a person does not prolong his words before a king as he does in his own home, and the King of kings of kings' gaze is constantly upon us; therefore it says, "let not [your heart] be hasty," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:37: One must be precise, however, for after all this verse appears redundant in its content — for "al tevahel al picha" already means that one should not utter speech from his mouth hastily, and this is [also the meaning of] "and let not your heart be hasty..."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:38: Therefore it appears that these are two distinct matters: the first regarding worldly speech, and the second regarding matters of holiness. Regarding what pertains to worldly speech, it says, "al tevahel al picha" — meaning: although you have permission to speak, that is, your mouth, which is at your discretion, it should not be in confusion and hastiness but with calm composure. And even in matters of holiness, when you stand before God, "let not [your heart] be hasty to utter a word before God" — and so it is explained in the Gemara (Berachot 5:1), that one should not pray immediately, but should first settle his mind and know before whom he stands, as they said, "one should not stand to pray except in a solemn frame of mind," and so on. And so it says in the Midrash (Yalkut, I Samuel, ch. 7, remez 146), that David said, "I would not pray before God until I had settled my mind," and we shall quote his entire wording below regarding prayer, please God. And even in occupation with Torah, one must sit with awe and direct what he utters from his mouth, as we shall elaborate in its place. And in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit 2a) it says that a word is worth a sela, silence is worth two — this too applies even in the matter of Torah. This is [the meaning of] "and let not your heart be hasty to utter a word before God" — meaning, when you stand before the Shechinah, which is when he is occupied with Torah and prayer, let him not be hasty.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:39: "For God is in heaven and you upon earth" — it is known that "Elohim" is a term of judgment and Judge, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explain (Shemot Rabbah 3:6): when I judge My world, I am called "Elohim." And in saying "in heaven," the intent is that He judges in heaven with the whole heavenly entourage that is in heaven, and therefore it does not say "for God is above the heavens," which would indicate His removal and elevation from them, but "in heaven" — to look upon and judge, as in "the Lord has established His throne in the heavens, and His kingdom rules over all" (Psalms 103:19). Further, "Elohim" numerically equals "HaKisei" (the Throne), and the intent is that His throne of judgment is in heaven, and the angels before Him, some on the right for merit, some on the left for guilt; and since the Holy One, blessed be He, judges a person's words with the whole heavenly entourage, whether his words are upright or not, it is fitting that they be few, in order to minimize the judgment against him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:40: Therefore it says all this in the term "Elohim," that everything is judged with the full measure of judgment, without any concession, as they said in the Midrash Vayikra Rabbah (Parashat Emor 26:7), in these words: Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] would recite the verses, and when he reached this verse he would weep: "For, lo, He who forms the mountains, and creates the wind, and declares unto man what is his thought (sicho)" (Amos 4:13). What is [the meaning of] "declares unto man what is his sicho"? Rabbi Huna in the name of Rabbi Yaavetz said, He forms the mountains and creates the wind. Rabbi Huna in the name of Rabbi Yaavetz said, another interpretation: "tohu, choshech, ve'afelah" (formlessness, darkness, and gloom) — even matters that have no substance, even light conversation that a man converses with his wife, are written in a person's record, and are read before him at the hour of his death; and who writes them? "He who makes the dawn (shachar) dark (eifah)" (Amos, ibid.) — so far their words. The reason speech is written by Him, blessed be He, is because speech is through the neshamah, as it is written, "and man became a living soul" (Genesis 2:7), which the Targum renders "and man became a speaking spirit," and it is known that the neshamah is from Him, blessed be He, as it is written, "and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life"; therefore, since it is the very substance of the neshamah that either blemishes through speech or is rectified through good speech, it is all written by Him, blessed be He, in order to punish or reward it measure for measure, according to His knowledge, blessed be He, which is not known to any creature, not to an angel nor a seraph.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:41: "And you upon earth" — it is precise in saying "and you upon (al) the earth," and not "and you in (ba') the earth" in the pattern of what it said, "for God is in heaven" — to resolve for us the difficulty we noted above. The matter is this: a person's essential dwelling, before Adam's sin, was in the Garden of Eden, removed from the materiality of this turbid body; but through his sin he became clothed in the body and the materiality of this world, and behold, he is, in his opinion, separated from holiness. However, the Holy One, blessed be He, placed in Adam, at the beginning of his creation, speech, beyond all other living creatures in this world — for through speech he is equal to the angels, as was explained above regarding the three bonds in a person: nefesh, ruach, neshamah, which are deed, speech, thought, and Rashbi explains that speech is from the holy living creatures, which is the level of ruach (Tikkunei Zohar 68b); and through speech a person has the power to cleave to holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:42: This is what King Solomon, peace be upon him, intended in saying, "Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of man ascends upward, and the spirit of the animal descends downward to the earth" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). For man, because of the speech within him, his spirit ascends upward, whereas the animal's spirit descends downward, because it returns to its foundation in mere Asiyah, since the power of speech, which is a divine power, was not placed within it — the divine power that was given to man, as it is said, "and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul," which the Targum renders, "and man became a speaking spirit."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:43: This is what it means by "and you upon (al) the earth" — for from the side of the neshamah and speech within you, you are removed from the earth and its materiality, meaning that you are not equal to the other living creatures on earth. Therefore, when a person speaks, whether words of holiness or mundane words, he should not think that he is speaking on earth and that he is physical, but rather that he is spiritual, speaking with the angels, since in speech he is equal to them. Therefore the verse need not say "for God is in heaven and on earth," for that would indicate that His providence is on earth to oversee the deeds done on earth from the side of the material act; but regarding speech, a person is bound above, and immediately upon uttering speech he is before God, and this God is in heaven. And this is the precision of the verse: "do not hasten to utter a word before God" — and because "before God" might imply [a God only] dwelling on earth, it guards against this and says that the God I mentioned to you is in heaven; and as for you, when you utter the word, you are [already] above the earth and removed from it — it follows that you are speaking before God in heaven, for the reason stated.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:44: "Therefore let your words be few" — since you stand above, before the King, it is not fitting to prolong your words before Him. And it is precise in saying "your words" — meaning, the words of the body, which are yours, and not the Holy One, blessed be He's; but words of praise and prayer and words of Torah, which are His, the King desires that you be before Him always, prolonging His praises and meditating on His Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:45: We have necessary confirmation for the truth of this introduction from the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, that speech has this level even more than other deeds a person performs — for other things a person does in deed, there are seven, "the eyes of the Lord range through all the earth" (cf. Zechariah 4:10), as is explained in Sabba, Parashat Mishpatim (107a), regarding "and what is evil in Your eyes I have done" (Psalms 51:6), that these [eyes] roam the world, and by them every commandment or transgression a person does is portrayed. However, regarding speech, Rashbi explains that the voice itself ascends above and is examined there — so it is explained in the Zohar, Parashat Lech Lecha (92a), in these words: Rabbi Yosei opened, "and your people, all of them righteous..." (Isaiah 60:21). Fortunate is Israel more than all other nations, for the Holy One, blessed be He, called them righteous — for it was taught: one hundred and twenty-eight thousand of the masters of wings go and fly through the whole world, and hear a voice and take hold of that voice — as we have learned, there is no word in the world that has no voice, and it goes and flies through the firmament, and the masters of wings take hold of it and raise that voice to their Masters of Judgment, and they judge it, whether for good or for evil, as it is written, "for a bird of the heavens shall carry the voice..." (Ecclesiastes 10:20) — so far his words. This shows that every speech has a voice and it ascends above through the firmament, and from there the masters of wings take the matter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:46: And in the Zohar (Parashat Metzora 55a), on the verse, "Hear the right, O Lord... [that proceeds] from lips without deceit" (Psalms 17:1), they add and say that the voice itself ascends and bursts through the firmament. They said, of blessed memory: what is [the meaning of] "from lips without deceit"? Rather, we have learned thus: every single word a person utters from his mouth ascends above and bursts through the firmaments, and enters the place it enters, and there that word is examined, whether it is a fitting word or not; if it is a fitting word, they bring it before the holy King to fulfill His will; if not, they turn it aside to the Other Side, to arouse through that word another spirit — so far his words. And so it is explained at the beginning of Parashat Naso, and we shall quote it below, please God.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:47: And so in the Zohar (Parashat Tzav 31b) it says that the matter dependent on speech arouses speech above, in these words: and should you say, what does a word arouse? Rather, thus it is written, "davar davar" ("and speaks [about the/a] matter") [Nach 13, likely referring to a verse containing this doubling] — that word arouses another word above, and it is called "davar," [as in] "the word of the Lord that was [to...]", and "the word of the Lord was precious [in those days]" (I Samuel 3:1), "by the word of the Lord the heavens were made" (Psalms 33:6) — for we have learned that that word ascends and bursts through the firmaments until it ascends to its place and arouses whatever it arouses, if good, good, if bad, bad, as it is written, "and you shall guard yourself from every [evil] thing (davar)" (Deuteronomy 23:10) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:48: However, this matter is difficult in light of what is explained in the Tikkunim (beginning of 131), that there are angels called "masters of wings" who are appointed over the voices of Torah, in these words: and there are commandments dependent on the mouth, appointed over the voices of Torah and over the utterances concerning which it is said, "for a bird of the heavens shall carry the voice, and that which has wings shall tell the matter" (Ecclesiastes 10:20) — so far his words. And it further says on (72a): and angels of whom it is said, "for a bird of the heavens shall carry the voice," who depend on the voice, "and that which has wings shall tell the matter," who depend on the speech — so far his words. It is difficult, since once the voice itself ascends and bursts through the firmament, why would these angels be needed?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:49: One might say that this ascending voice certainly has some aspect of materiality from the side of the person, who is in this physical mode of "doing" (asiyah); therefore the masters of wings take hold of it in order to refine it, so that it ascends to the proper place — whether it is the breath of Torah or prayer, that it ascend higher and higher to unify; and if the ascending voice is a voice concerning worldly matters, they judge it as needed. With this resolution we must also explain what is said in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel 201b), that there are several angels who raise the prayer from firmament to firmament — why would they be needed? Rather, certainly to refine it from materiality so that it ascend higher and higher to unify.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:50: It might further be said that "for God is in heaven" is as explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (256a), in the mystery of the Name "Elohim," in these words: "Elohim" testifies to His own Godhood — that there is "Elohim" and "the God of gods," and He is the God over all, and there is no god above Him — so far his words. And "in heaven" can be understood by what is explained in the Tikkunim (end of 3), that the Cause of all shines in the ten sefirot of Atzilut, and so on, and in the ten spheres of the firmament, and does not change in any place. This is the intent of "for God is in heaven" — meaning, that His Godhood and light shine equally throughout all the heavens as one, as it says, that He shines in the ten spheres of the firmament, and so on. Now, this certainly indicates providence.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:51: It might further be said, "for God is in heaven," that "Elohim" is known to be the supernal Imma, and her seat is in "the heavens," which are the three Patriarchs — the intent being that she decrees no decree except by the court of three, who are the three Patriarchs, so that the matter is judged for right and for left, and afterward the third decides. In the same pattern, a person who is on the earth, when he utters a word, should first weigh it in the scales of reason, for right, for left, and for a decision, and by this his words will be few. I have further hidden matters regarding this verse written with me, but it is enough what we have elaborated for practical benefit.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:52: Now, the particular aspects explained in this verse obligate a person to minimize his words — whether in the aspect of the mystery of "hevel" explained, or in the aspect of the five points of articulation fixed in his mouth, that there be no adhesion in them, or in the aspect of voice and speech, or in the aspect of the refinement of the voice and speech ascending above to be judged as explained, or in the aspect of the constant providence over him — he must minimize his words in worldly matters.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:53: And with this, this chapter is concluded:
